parole.significato: An informer; a criminal who informs on other criminals to the authorities.

parole.significato: A gem engraved with the word Abrasax or Abraxas.

parole.significato: Hell; the bottomless pit; primeval chaos; a confined subterranean ocean.

parole.testo: From Late Latin acatalēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκατάληκτος (akatálēktos, “leaving off”).

parole.significato: Guilty of apostasy.

parole.significato: A member of a sect in the primitive church who celebrated the Lord's Supper with bread and cheese.

parole.significato: self-discipline, particularly as a religious observance; asceticism.

parole.significato: To pave with asphalt.

parole.significato: The mucous membrane that lines the uterus in mammals and in which fertilized eggs are implanted.
parole.testo: From endo- (“inner”) + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”). Compare μήτρᾱ (mḗtrā, “womb”).

parole.significato: An injection of fluid into the large intestine by way of the rectum, usually for medical purposes.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin enema, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

parole.significato: The complete realisation and final form of some potential concept or function; the conditions under which a potential t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia), coined by Aristotle from ἐντελής (entelḗs, “complete, finished, perfect”) (from τέλος (télos, “end, fruition, accomplishment”)) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”).

parole.significato: The insertion of a phoneme, letter, or syllable into a word, usually to satisfy the phonological constraints of a langu…
parole.testo: Middle of 16th century: via Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἐπένθεσις (epénthesis), from ἐπεντίθημι (epentíthēmi, “to insert”), from ἐπί (epí) + ἐντίθημι (entíthēmi, “to put in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, place”).

parole.significato: An activity, process, or state that is the result of another; a by-product, a consequence.
parole.testo: From epi- (prefix meaning ‘above, on, over; in addition to’) + phenomenon. Phenomenon is derived from Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing that appears in one’s view; appearance; phenomenon”), a noun use of the neuter singular form of φαινόμενος (

parole.significato: Of or relating to the affairs of a bishop in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: From Middle English episcopal, from Late Latin episcopālis, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watchman, overseer”).

parole.significato: Bishops seen as a group.
parole.testo: From Late Latin episcopatus, from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “watching over”).

parole.significato: a hurried accumulation or enumeration of several points.
parole.testo: From Late Latin epitrochasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτροχασμός (epitrokhasmós), from ἐπιτροχάζω (epitrokházō, “run swiftly over”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech whereby a question is asked in confident expectation of a negative answer.
parole.testo: From Late Latin erotesis, from Ancient Greek ἐρώτησις (erṓtēsis), from ἐρωτάω (erōtáō, “I question”).

parole.significato: Moral, relating to morals.
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, from Late Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθῐκός (ēthĭkós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the study of ethics.
parole.testo: From ethic + -al, from Late Latin ethicus (“moral, ethical”), from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: Of a doctrine, information, etc.: suitable to be imparted to the public without secrecy or other reservations.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient city of Gadara (near modern-day Umm Qais, in Jordan).
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gadarēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γαδαρηνός (Gadarēnós, “inhabitant of Gadara”), from Γάδαρα (Gádara, “Gadara”, now “Umm Qais”).

parole.significato: A mathematician who specializes in geometry.
parole.testo: From Middle English gemeter, geometer, ultimately from Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + μετρέω (metréō, “to measure”).

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Gerasa
parole.testo: From the Late Latin Gerasēnus, Gergesēnus, from the Ancient Greek Γερασηνός (Gerasēnós), Γεργεσηνός (Gergesēnós), from Γέρασα (Gérasa), Γέργεσα (Gérgesa). By surface analysis, Gerasa + -ene.

parole.significato: A hinge joint.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek γίγγλυμος (gínglumos, “hinge”).

parole.significato: Relating to goth music or people.
parole.testo: From gothic rock, first used by John Stickney in reference to The Doors in 1967 and used by the late 1970s to describe the musical scene that gave rise to the goth subculture, both from a supposed aesthetic similarity to dark and moody 19th century gothic fiction and earlier gothic art and architect

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Goths or their language.
parole.testo: From Late Latin gothicus (“Gothic, barbaric”), from Ancient Greek Γοτθικός (Gotthikós), from Ancient Greek Γότθοι (Gótthoi, “Goths”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), proposed to derive from unattested Gothic *𐌲𐌿𐍄𐌰 (*guta). parole.significato: Abnormal curvature or hooked appearance.
parole.testo: From Late Latin grȳpōsis (“hooking”) (from grȳpus (“hook-nosed”)), from Ancient Greek γρυπῶσις (grupôsis, “hooking”), from γρύπεσθαι (grúpesthai, “become hooked”), from γρύπος (grúpos, “hook-nosed”).

parole.significato: The dugong.
parole.testo: From Late Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls, “sea”) + κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden”).

parole.significato: A group of seven.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hebdomada (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), hebdomas (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, suffix forming abstract nouns of

parole.significato: Texts or artifacts containing Hebrew writing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hebraica, neuter plural of hebraicus (“Hebrew”), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew”) (likely through Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”)), traditionally from עֵבֶר ('éver, “Eber”), the ancestor of the Israelites. By surface an

parole.significato: A headache affecting one side of the head.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hemicrania (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (from whence also cranium). Cognate to megrim and migraine, which also derive from the Latin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the liver.
parole.testo: From Middle English epatik, from Late Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “of the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).

parole.significato: Irregularly declined or inflected.
parole.testo: From Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Hibiscus, especially Hibiscus syriacus, found in tropical to temperate regions, of some…
parole.testo: From Late Latin hibiscus, from Latin hibiscum, from Ancient Greek ἰβίσκος (ibískos, “marsh mallow”), probably ultimately from Gaulish.

parole.significato: A mythological creature with the front head and forelimbs of a horse and the rear of a fish.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea-monster”)). The anatomy sense is so named from its resemblance to the seahorse. By surface analysis, hippo- + campus.

parole.significato: Showing a degree of correspondence or similarity.
parole.testo: From Late Latin homologus, from Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, reckoning”). Compare homo- (“same”) and -ous (adjectival suffix). From 1655, in the mathematical sense. See also homolog, homologue.

parole.significato: One of a race of people living in the extreme north, beyond the north wind.
parole.testo: From Late Latin hyperboreanus, cognate with Classical Latin hyperboreus, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβόρεος (huperbóreos), composed of ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βόρειος (bóreios, “northern”). By surface analysis, nearly hyper- + boreal. See also Ὑπερβόρεοι (Huperbóreoi).

parole.significato: The symbol "‐", typically used to join two or more words to form a compound term, or to indicate that a word has been s…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔φέν (hŭphén, “in one, as a single word”), univerbation of ῠ̔φ’ ἕν (hŭph’ hén, “under one”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, “under”) + ἕν (hén, “one”), neuter of εἷς (heîs, “one”).

parole.significato: A term of endearment, often a diminutive; a pet name.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin hypocorisma, a loan from Ancient Greek ὑποκόρισμα (hupokórisma), ὑποκορισμός (hupokorismós, “pet name”), from ὑποκορίζεσθαι (hupokorízesthai), ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to use a pet name; to act in a childish manner”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, prefix indicating a small degree)

parole.significato: Relating to, or having the characteristics of, an icon.
parole.testo: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

parole.significato: Divination by idols, images or figures.
parole.testo: First element is from Late Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”). Second element is from Latin -mantīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā). Equivalent to idol + -mancy.

parole.significato: To stupefy by doping with chemical substances such as alcohol.
parole.testo: First attested in 1450, in Middle English; from Middle English intoxicaten, from intoxicat(e) (“(of a weapon or drug) smeared, anointed or filled with poison; (of a human being, animal) poisoned, intoxicated”, also used as the past participle of intoxicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed fro

parole.significato: Characterized by or constituting (any kind of) irony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the erect phallus that was carried in bacchic processions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ithyphallicus, from Ancient Greek ἰθυφαλλικός (ithuphallikós), from ῑ̓θῠ́φαλλος (īthŭ́phallos, “phallus carried in festivals of Bacchus; ode sung in honour of the phallus; dance accompanying such an ode; dancer performing such a dance”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix forming adjecti

parole.significato: A breed of multihorned sheep.
parole.testo: From Middle English Iacob, from Late Latin Iācōbus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάκωβος (Iákōbos), from Biblical Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (yaʿăqōḇ, literally “May He Heel”), from the third-person singular masculine imperfective form of the Semitic verb "to heel" (with various meanings), in turn from עָקֵב (ʿāqēḇ, “hee

parole.significato: The highest form of worship, named adoration, properly given to the triune God alone.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service,” “worship”), from λατρευειν (latreuein, “wait on,” “serve with prayer”).

parole.significato: A number of hermitages or cells in the same neighborhood occupied by anchorites who were under the same superior
parole.testo: From the Late Latin laura, from Ancient Greek λαύρα (laúra, “lane, path”).

parole.significato: Divination by interpreting the sound or effect of an object or substance (commonly a gem) falling into a body of water.
parole.testo: From Late Latin lecanomantia, from Ancient Greek λεκανομαντείᾱ (lekanomanteíā), from λεκάνη (lekánē, “dish, pan”).

parole.significato: A member of the Hebrew tribe of Levi, particularly in its role as a priestly caste.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Levītēs, Lēvīta, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Λευῑ̈́της (Leuī̈́tēs). By surface analysis, Levi + -ite.

parole.significato: A gemstone, supposed to have been a form of agate
parole.testo: Likely derived from the ancient region of Liguria in northwestern Italy, from Middle English lygire, ligury, lugre, from Late Latin ligūrius, from Ancient Greek λιγύριον (ligúrion) or λυγκούριον (lunkoúrion).

parole.significato: A figure of speech whereby something is stated by denying its opposite.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs, literally “plainness”), from λιτός (litós, “simple”).

parole.significato: Patience or tolerance in the face of adversity; forbearance, long-suffering.
parole.testo: From Late Latin longanimitās, from longanimis, translating Ancient Greek μακροθυμία (makrothumía).

parole.significato: magnesium oxide
parole.testo: From Middle English magnesia, from Late Latin magnesia, from Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía), after Μαγνησία (Magnēsía), a name of several cities (in Thessaly, Lydia, and Asia Minor). Doublet of Magnesia, magnesium, and manganese, and related to magnet.

parole.significato: A handful.
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin manipulus (“bundle, handful; drachm”) (see further at etymology 1), modelled on Ancient Greek δράγμα (drágma, “bundle, handful; sheaf”) which was confused with δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “drachm”).

parole.significato: Food miraculously produced for the Israelites in the desert in the book of Exodus.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Old English, from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מן (mān, “'manna”).

parole.significato: A condition of chronic undernourishment especially in children, caused by a diet deficient in calories or the inability…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin marasmus, from Ancient Greek μᾰρᾰσμός (mărăsmós, “withering”, noun).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or from the ancient city of Megalopolis (now Megalopoli) in Greece.
parole.testo: A variant of Megalopolitan; analysable as Megapolis + -itan. Megapolis is derived from Late Latin megapolis, from Ancient Greek μεγα- (mega-, “prefix meaning ‘large’”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”).

parole.significato: Deep sadness or gloom; melancholy
parole.testo: From Late Latin melancholia, which was in turn borrowed from the Ancient Greek medical term μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medici

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Melissa, especially lemon balm (Melissa officinalis), often used medicinally.
parole.testo: From Late Latin melissa, from Ancient Greek μέλισσα (mélissa, “bee”), because the plant attracts bees.

parole.significato: The mesentery.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mesenterium and its source, Ancient Greek μεσεντέριον (mesentérion).

parole.significato: The membrane that attaches the intestines to the wall of the abdomen, maintaining their position in the abdominal cavit…
parole.testo: From Late Latin mesenterium, from Ancient Greek μεσεντέρῐον (mesentérĭon), from μέσος (mésos, “middle”) + ἔντερον (énteron, “gut”).

parole.significato: Mesenteric.
parole.testo: From Late Latin meseraicus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μεσαραϊκός (mesaraïkós) (in Galen), from μεσάραιον (mesáraion, “mesaraeum”).

parole.significato: A change from one subject to another.
parole.testo: From Late Latin metabasis, from Ancient Greek μετάβασις (metábasis, “a change, a transition”), from μεταβαίνω (metabaínō, “I cross”), from μετά (metá) and βαίνω (baínō, “I move”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-.

parole.significato: The transposition of letters, syllables or sounds within a word.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis), from μετά (metá, “among”) + θέσις (thésis, “placement”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Greek city-states, a resident alien who did not have the rights of a citizen and who paid a tax for the righ…
parole.testo: From Late Latin metycus (also metoecus), from Ancient Greek μέτοικος (métoikos, “foreigner, metic”).

parole.significato: The use of a single characteristic or part of an object, concept or phenomenon to identify the entire object, concept,…
parole.testo: From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: The mother (founding) polis (city state) of a colony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”), from μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city (state)”). By surface analysis, metro- + -polis. Doublet of metropole.

parole.significato: A bishop empowered to oversee other bishops; an archbishop.
parole.testo: From Late Latin metropolitanus, from Ancient Greek μητροπολίτης (mētropolítēs).

parole.significato: Synonym of mithridate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mithridatium, from Latin Mithridātīus (“of or related to Mithridates”), from Mithridātēs + -ius, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridate, mithridatum, and mithridaticon.

parole.significato: Synonym of mithridate.
parole.testo: From Late Latin mithridatum, variant of mithridatium, from Latin Mithridātīus (“of or related to Mithridates”), from Mithridātēs + -ius, from Ancient Greek Μιθριδάτης (Mithridátēs), the Greek form of the name of Mithridates VI of Pontus. Doublet of mithridate, mithridatium, and mithridaticon.

parole.significato: Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mnemonicus or its etymon Ancient Greek μνημονῐκός (mnēmonĭkós, “pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). parole.significato: Consisting of one syllable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, monosyllable + -ic or mono- + syllabic.

parole.significato: The way in which an organism (or an organ) changes form during development.
parole.testo: From Late Latin morphosis, from Ancient Greek μόρφωσις (mórphōsis, “shaping”).

parole.significato: A shrew or ferret.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mygale (“field mouse”) (Vetus Latina), from Ancient Greek μυγαλέη (mugaléē, “shrew”) (used in the Septuagint to translate Hebrew אֲנָקָה, now generally thought to indicate a gecko or similar small reptile).

parole.significato: The smooth muscle forming the wall of the uterus.
parole.testo: From myo- + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”).

parole.significato: Anything transmitted by word of mouth, such as a fable, legend, narrative, story, or tale (especially a poetic tale).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”). Doublet of myth. The plural form mythoi is from Ancient Greek μῦθοι (mûthoi), and the form mythoses from mythos + -es.

parole.significato: Synonym of mythos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mythus, from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”).

parole.significato: Modern, new-fangled.
parole.testo: From Late Latin neotericus, from Hellenistic Greek νεωτερικός (neōterikós), from comparative of Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”).

parole.significato: A Nicolaitan.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Nicolaita, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Νικολαΐτης (Nikolaḯtēs), from Νικόλαος (Nikólaos, “Nicolas”); Nicolas of Antioch was associated with the sect, although the word may have come from a different allegorical use of the name.

parole.significato: Of an infection or its cause: arising from the environment of, or treatment in, a hospital.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin nosocomīum (“hospital, infirmary”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Nosocomīum is borrowed from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital, infirmary”), from νοσοκομέω (nosokoméō, “to tend the sick”) + -εῖον (-eîon, suf

parole.significato: A spring of fresh water, surrounded by a fertile region of vegetation, in a desert.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25 Compare Sahidic Coptic ⲟⲩⲁϩⲉ (ouahe) and Arabic وَاحَة (wāḥa).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to oligarchy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarch + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the town of Olympia in Elis, Greece; Olympic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin Olympianus (“Olympic”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, or forming agent nouns). Olympianus is derived from Latin Olympia (“town in Elis, Greece, where the ancient Olympic Games were held”) + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’); and Oly

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin oolithus; the Latin word was coined by the German doctor and mineralogist Franz Ernst Brückmann (1697–1753) as a translation of German Rogenstein (“oolite”) (Rogen (“fish roe”) + Stein (“stone”)). parole.significato: A person, especially a minor, both or (rarely) one of whose parents have died.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos. parole.significato: A mixture of honey, water, and vinegar, boiled to a syrup, sometimes mixed with herbs or spices.
parole.testo: From Middle English oximel, from Late Latin oxymel, oxymeli (“acid and honey”), from Ancient Greek ὀξύμελι (oxúmeli).

parole.significato: Emphatic repetition of a word or phrase.
parole.testo: From Late Latin palilogia (“palilogy”), from Ancient Greek παλιλογία (palilogía, “palilogy”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + -λογία (-logía, “pertaining to speech, discourse”) or -λόγος (-lógos, “word, speech”).

parole.significato: An Ancient Greek stringed instrument, a kind of lute with three strings that were stopped with a fingerboard to alter t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin pandura, from Ancient Greek πανδοῦρα (pandoûra), a Pre-Greek/substrate loan. Doublet of mandola.

parole.significato: A pattern, a way of doing something; especially a pattern of thought, a system of beliefs, a conceptual framework.
parole.testo: From Middle English paradygme, from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”), from παραδείκνυμι (paradeíknumi, “I show [beside] or compare”) + -μα (-ma, suffix forming nouns concerning the results of actions). Doublet of paradigma.

parole.significato: A written pattern of inflection for parts of speech, especially organized into a tabular form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”). As a loanword in both languages, paradigma typically maintains the Greek plural form in both Latin and English. Doublet of paradigm.

parole.significato: The addition of a sound, syllable or letter to the end of a word, either through natural development or as a grammatica…
parole.testo: From Late Latin paragoge, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).

parole.significato: A play on words; a pun.

parole.significato: A woman's property which was not made a part of her marriage dower, but remained her own.

parole.significato: Government by five persons.

parole.significato: A section of text forming a coherent thought, suitable for use in a speech.

parole.significato: A sudden reversal of fortune as a plot point in Classical tragedy.
parole.testo: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: The herb vervain (Verbena officinalis).
parole.testo: From Late Latin peristerion, from Ancient Greek περιστέριον (peristérion).

parole.significato: A phase (of the moon, a planet etc.).
parole.testo: From Late Latin phasis, or its source, Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”).

parole.significato: A thing or being, event or process, perceptible through senses; or a fact or occurrence thereof.
parole.testo: From Late Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”), neuter present middle participle of φαίνω (phaínō, “I show”).

parole.significato: Φ, the 21st letter of the Euclidean and modern Greek alphabet, usually romanized as "ph".
parole.testo: From Late Latin phi, from Ancient Greek φεῖ (pheî).

parole.significato: Benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of humankind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía). By surface analysis, phil- + -anthropy.

parole.significato: A short written or spoken expression.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”), from φράζω (phrázō, “to tell, express”).

parole.significato: All of the organisms descending from a given common ancestor, regarded as a race, tribe, vel sim.; a clade.

parole.significato: The symbol ¶.
parole.testo: Probably an alteration of Middle English pylcrafte, modification of Late Latin paragraphus, itself from the Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).

parole.significato: Designating a mode lying a perfect fourth below the authentic form.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plagalis, from plaga, from plagius, from Byzantine Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios, “plagal”), πλάγιος (plágios, “oblique”).

parole.significato: Slanted, oblique.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plagio-, from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios, “oblique”).

parole.significato: Protoplasm.

parole.significato: A state of matter consisting of partially ionized gas and electrons.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plasma (“mold”), from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”).

parole.significato: Redundancy in wording.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

parole.significato: An excessive amount or number; an abundance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra, from Ancient Greek πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “fullness, satiety”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to be full”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Suffering from plethora; ruddy in complexion, congested or swollen with blood.
parole.testo: From Late Latin plethoricus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πληθωρικός (plēthōrikós), from πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “plethora”). By surface analysis, plethora + -ic.

parole.significato: long-lasting; chronic.
parole.testo: From Late Latin polychronius (“long-lived”), from Ancient Greek πολῠχρόνῐος (polŭkhrónĭos, “long-lived”).

parole.significato: The condition of having more than one spouse or marriage partner at one time.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1591, from Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), itself from πολύγαμος (polúgamos, “married to many”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). Relates to modern prefix and suffix poly- + -gamy.

parole.significato: Synonym of polypody: any fern of the genus Polypodium.
parole.testo: From Late Latin polypodium, from Ancient Greek πολυπόδιον (polupódion), from πολυ- (polu-, “poly-, many”) + πούς (poús, “-pod, foot”) + -ιον (-ion, “-ium”). Later reinforced by the translingual scientific use of Polypodium.

parole.significato: An elder, priest, pastor, or minister in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of prester and priest.

parole.significato: The home of a Roman Catholic parish priest.
parole.testo: From Middle English presbetory, presbytory (“part of church reserved for clergy”), from Late Latin presbyterium (“group of presbyters, part of church reserved for clergy”), from Ancient Greek πρεσβῠτέρῐον (presbŭtérĭon, “group of presbyters”), from πρεσβῠ́τερος (presbŭ́teros, “elder, priest”) + -ῐον

parole.significato: The first part of a play, in which the setting and characters are introduced.
parole.testo: From Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis), from προτείνω (proteínō, “put forward, tender, propose”), from πρό (pró) + τείνω (teínō, “stretch”).

parole.significato: An ancient Persian temple devoted to fire.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pyreum, from Ancient Greek πυρεῖον (pureîon).

parole.significato: The priestess of the oracle of Apollo at Delphi.
parole.testo: From Late Latin pythonissa, from Ancient Greek Πυθία (Puthía). Compare Pythia.

parole.significato: Synonym of Rachel sandwich.

parole.significato: Excessive sexual desire, found in a man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin satyriasis, from Ancient Greek σατυρίασις (saturíasis).

parole.significato: Having sides all unequal in length.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin scalēnus (“of unequal sides”), from Ancient Greek σκᾰληνός (skălēnós, “uneven, unequal”).

parole.significato: shadow-boxing; fighting that is futile or make-believe
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciamachia, and its source, Hellenistic Ancient Greek σκιαμαχία (skiamakhía), from σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μάχη (mákhē, “battle”).

parole.significato: Neuralgia of the sciatic nerve, characterised by pain radiating down through the buttocks and the back of the thigh.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Late Latin sciatica, feminine of sciaticus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: divination using shadows
parole.testo: From Late Latin sciomantia, from Ancient Greek σκιά (skiá, “shadow”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: An area of impaired or lost vision within a visual field otherwise in a good (or at least healthy) state.

parole.significato: A member of a modern people that speak a Semitic language.

parole.significato: A silk gland, as in the silkworms.
parole.testo: Late Latin sericterium, from Ancient Greek σηρικόν (sērikón, “silk”).

parole.significato: A skeleton.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sceletus, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (skeletós).

parole.significato: Pertaining to alchemy; alchemical, especially regarding medicine.
parole.testo: From Late Latin spagyricus, from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō, “I draw, pull”) + ἀγείρω (ageírō, “I assemble”).

parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphinctēr (“the muscle of the anus”), from Ancient Greek σφῐγκτήρ (sphĭnktḗr, “lace, band; contractile muscle”), ultimately of Pre-Greek origin. Possibly related to sphinx (“the strangler”).

parole.significato: The science of measuring the volume of solids or solid bodies.
parole.testo: From Late Latin, from Ancient Greek στερεομετρία (stereometría), from στερεός (stereós, “solid”).

parole.significato: A brief summary of the major points of a written work, either as prose or as a table; an abridgment or condensation of…

parole.significato: A constituent segment within a text, such as a word or a phrase that forms a syntactic unit.
parole.testo: From Late Latin syntagma, from Ancient Greek σύνταγμα (súntagma, “orderly arrangement”), from συντάσσω (suntássō, “arrange together”, “to order”).

parole.significato: A set of rules that govern how words are combined to form phrases and sentences.
parole.testo: Partly from Late Latin syntaxis and partly from its etymon, Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis), from σύν (sún, “together”) + τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”). Doublet of syntaxis.

parole.significato: Syntax.
parole.testo: From the Late Latin syntaxis, from the Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis). Doublet of syntax.

parole.significato: An alignment of three celestial bodies (for example, the Sun, Earth, and Moon) such that one body is directly between t…
parole.testo: From Late Latin sȳzygia (“a conjunction”), from Ancient Greek συζυγία (suzugía, “a union, a yoke, a pair”). This word was recognized as English in 1847 (in its astronomical meaning).

parole.significato: Redundant use of words, a pleonasm, an unnecessary and tedious repetition.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología) from ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”). By surface analysis, tauto- + -logy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to construction or to architecture.

parole.significato: A form of magic designed to allow for worship or conjuration of, or communication with spirits or deities.
parole.testo: From Late Latin theūrgia, from Ancient Greek θεουργίᾱ (theourgíā, “sorcery”), from θεός (theós, “god”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, the- + -urgy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Titans, a race of giant gods in Greek mythology.

parole.significato: The insertion of one or more words between the components of a compound word.
parole.testo: From Late Latin tmēsis, from Ancient Greek τμῆσις (tmêsis, “a cutting”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”). First attested in 1586.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin tragus, from Ancient Greek τράγος (trágos, “he-goat; part of the ear”); with reference to a tuft of hair, likened to a goat’s beard, that may grow on the tragus, especially in older men.

parole.significato: A quadrilateral with two sides parallel.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin trapezium, borrowed from Ancient Greek τρᾰπέζῐον (trăpézĭon, “irregular quadrilateral”, literally “small table”), from τράπεζα (trápeza, “table”) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive suffix). First attested in 1570. Doublet of trapeze.

parole.significato: Mean; worthless.
parole.testo: From Late Latin triobolaris, from Latin triobolus (“a coin worth three oboli”), from Ancient Greek τρῐώβολον (trĭṓbolon). Literally, "having the value of three oboli".

parole.significato: Either of the two parallels of latitude 23°26′ north and south of the equator; the farthest points at which the sun can…
parole.testo: From Late Latin tropicus (“of or pertaining to the solstice, as a noun, one of the tropics”), from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós, “of or pertaining to a turn or change; or the solstice; or a trope or figure; tropic; tropical; etc.”), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turn; solstice; trope”).

parole.significato: Capturing the overall sense of a thing.
parole.testo: From Late Latin typicalis, from Latin typicus (“typical”), from Ancient Greek τυπικός (tupikós, “of or pertaining to a type, conformable, typical”), from τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), equivalent to typic + -al and type + -ical.
